# Microsoft 365 Copilot Now Lets You Pick Your AI: What to Know

> **In short:** Microsoft 365 Copilot is introducing a model picker, so you can choose which underlying AI handles each task — a fast model for quick drafts, a reasoning model for trickier work. For everyday users, the AI inside Word, Outlook, and Excel can now behave differently depending on the job you give it.

Last week you asked Copilot to summarise a long email thread, and it gave you three useful bullets. Then you asked it to draft a careful reply to a tricky complaint, and the result felt a bit flat. Soon, you might be able to pick which **AI model** (the underlying engine that actually does the thinking) handles each request — a bit like choosing a different chef for a different dish.

## Why one AI isn't perfect for everything

Every AI model is built with trade-offs. Some are trained to be fast and cheap — they spin through a long document and give you a summary in seconds. Others are built for **deeper reasoning** — they think through problems step by step and tend to get trickier tasks right.

No single model is best at everything. A model that's great at quick summarising might be sloppy at careful analysis. A model built for careful analysis might be overkill (and slow) when you just want a quick rewrite of a sentence.

It's the same reason your phone has different camera modes: portrait for faces, landscape for scenery. Different tools for different jobs.

## What's changing in Microsoft 365

Microsoft is rolling out a **model picker** inside Copilot. Instead of being stuck with one default model, you'll see a small choice — usually one tuned for speed, one tuned for reasoning, and sometimes a creative writing model.

For organisations, there's also a **governance layer** (the rules an IT team sets up to control how AI is used at work). Admins can decide which models are available, which are locked down, and which departments can use which. That matters because some AI models handle sensitive data differently, and some are only safe to use inside certain regions or plans.

For the everyday user, the practical change is simpler: a small dropdown or selector near the prompt box, letting you swap models when you want a different kind of help.

## How to think about picking a model

A rough guide:

- **Fast / default model** — quick summarising, simple rewrites, drafting a quick email. Good for everyday "just get something on the page" tasks.
- **Reasoning model** — careful analysis, tricky logic, working through a complex spreadsheet, drafting something where accuracy matters more than speed.
- **Creative model** — brainstorming, opening lines, slogans, marketing copy.

You don't need to memorise this. Start with the default and only switch when the answer feels wrong or shallow for the task.

## What this means for you

- **If you use Microsoft 365 for everyday tasks** (email, documents, study): you don't have to do anything. The default model will keep doing what it does today. When you want a different result, look for a model selector near the prompt box — try a reasoning model for trickier jobs and a creative one for brainstorming.

- **If you use Copilot at work**: your IT team may set which models you can see, so you might not get the full list. Ask them what's available. Treat sensitive information the way you always have — model choice doesn't change how careful you need to be with private data.

- **If you're a small business owner or admin**: you can now match models to tasks rather than paying for one model to handle every job. Think of it as choosing the right tool from a toolbox, not buying one tool that has to do everything.

## Wrap-up

Copilot picking the right AI model is mostly an upgrade you don't have to think about — but if you want more control, you now have it. Try the default for your next routine task, then experiment with switching models the next time the answer doesn't feel quite right. That's the simplest way to learn which model fits which job for you.
